newsitem.title: PAKISTAN: FEATURE-Sectarian tension grips Pakistani town.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE-Sectarian tension grips Pakistani town.

text.p: Paramilitary troops are patrolling this remote tribal town in northwestern Pakistan, a month after clashes between well-armed Sunni and Shi'ite Moslem tribesmen killed about 100 people.
A night curfew remains in force in Parachinar, in the Kurram Valley west of the city of Peshawar, near the Afghan border.
The town seems calm, but tense, and the scars of last month's violence are still visible.

The blood-stained satchel of Ibrahim, a 13-year-old school boy, lies in the headmaster's office where he was shot by teenaged schoolmates. Ibrahim and Saleem, 11, another pupil at the school, were among the first victims of the bloodletting.
Witnesses said fellow-students shot them dead on September 10, sparking a week of clashes between Sunni and Shi'ite tribes.

The Shi'ite headmaster, Israr Hussain, was killed in his office when he tried to save Ibrahim and Saleem, both Sunnis, from armed Shi'ite pupils avenging what they believed to have been derogatory remarks against their version of Islam.
"Sectarian clashes flared up in Parachinar town and neighbouring villages after the school incident," said Kamran Qureshi, the Islamabad-appointed Political Agent of the area.
Within 30 minutes of the school killings, the town became a battlefield in which rival tribesmen used mortars, rocket launchers and missiles, as well as Kalashnikov assault rifles.

Religious militants targeted each other's mosques, now scarred by battle and guarded by the Thal Scouts, a paramilitary force under the interior minmistry, who say they found big arms caches in the places of worship.
"It was a frenzy," said an officer of the Thal Scouts. "People were dragged out and slaughtered. Shops and houses were burned and looted. Women and children were not spared."
"About 100 people were killed and more than 100 wounded in five or six days of sectarian clashes in and around Parachinar," Qureshi said. More than 200 people were arrested.
Each side accuses the other of starting the unrest.
"It was not spontaneous. The Shi'ites launched a planned attack to push Sunnis out of the town," said Haji Sirajuddin, president of the Sunni Aqwam Ahle-Sunnat-o-al-Jamaat group.

Haji Gulab Hussain, president of the rival Shi'ite Tanzim-ul-Momineen, said his organisation had suffered great losses. "It is a false accusation that we started the fight. We only retaliated for Sunni attacks," he added.
The authorities in this rugged land, where ancient tribal law prevails and the Pakistani government exerts only loose control, have not assigned blame for the violence.
"Our immediate concern is relief work in remote areas, recovery of kidnapped people and complete restoration of power, water and telephone lines," said Qureshi.
Shi'ites are a majority in Parachinar, a market town serving the Kurram valley, while Sunnis dominate nearby villages and the town of Sadda in the southern part of the valley.
Conflict between the two sects stretches back at least as far as the era of British rule which ended in 1947, officials say.

"One reason for the rift is that Sunnis want to assert their position in Parachinar and buy property, but the Shi'ite majority, belonging mostly to the Touri tribe, does not want to share with Sunni tribes the prized lands they were given by the British," said a government official in Peshawar.

Qureshi said the sects had fought at least seven major battles since 1947. "For each side it is a jihad (holy war) and the religious leaders always keep the temperature of their followers high," he said.
A paramilitary officer said sectarian militancy elsewhere in Pakistan had fuelled tension in Kurram, where tribal traditions can keep old feuds simmering for generations.
He said house-to-house searches in Parachinar had uncovered hidden arms and ammunition ranging from Kalashnikovs to mortars, anti-aircraft guns, rocket launchers and anti-tank mines.
"This ammunition is enough to wage at least two months of war in this area," a senior Thal Scouts officer said.
"We have disarmed most people in Parachinar town, but it won't take them long to re-arm once the curfew is lifted. It is impossible to seal Kurram's border with Afghanistan," he said.
